q: In which year was William Shakespeare baptized at Holy Trinity Church, Stratford-upon-Avon?
e: William Shakespeare was baptized on 26 April 1564 (traditionally celebrated as born on 23 April 1564) and died on 23 April 1616. His parents were John Shakespeare and Mary Arden, and he married Anne Hathaway in 1582.

q: How many plays were included in the First Folio (1623) of Shakespeare's works, compiled by John Heminges and Henry Condell?
e: The First Folio (Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies, 1623) contained 36 plays, omitting 'Pericles, Prince of Tyre' (added in the Third Folio, 1664). It was printed by Isaac Jaggard and Edward Blount.

q: How many sonnets did William Shakespeare publish in the 1609 Quarto (printed by Thomas Thorpe)?
e: Shakespeare's 154 sonnets follow the English/Shakespearean rhyme scheme (abab cdcd efef gg). Sonnets 1–126 are addressed to the Fair Youth, 127–152 to the Dark Lady, and 153–154 are adaptations of Greek epigrams on Cupid.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of A.C. Bradley's 'Four Great Tragedies' of Shakespeare?
e: Shakespeare's Four Great Tragedies are Hamlet (1600–01), Othello (1604), King Lear (1605–06), and Macbeth (1606), analyzed in A.C. Bradley's 'Shakespearean Tragedy' (1904). Julius Caesar (1599) is classified among the Roman Plays.

q: In which play does the famous soliloquy beginning "To be, or not to be, that is the question" appear?
e: Prince Hamlet delivers this iconic meditation on life, death, and inaction in Act III, Scene 1 of 'Hamlet'. Ophelia is present nearby while Claudius and Polonius eavesdrop behind the arras.

q: What is the subtitle of Shakespeare's comedy 'Twelfth Night'?
e: 'Twelfth Night, or What You Will' (c. 1601–02) is set in Illyria and features Viola (disguised as Cesario), Duke Orsino, Olivia, Malvolio, and the clown Feste. It opens with "If music be the food of love, play on."

q: To whom did William Shakespeare dedicate his narrative poems 'Venus and Adonis' (1593) and 'The Rape of Lucrece' (1594)?
e: Both 'Venus and Adonis' (6-line stanzas, ababcc — called "the first heir of my invention") and 'The Rape of Lucrece' (Rhyme Royal, ababbcc) were dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, 3rd Earl of Southampton.

q: Who is the villainous ensign who manipulates Othello into murdering Desdemona in 'Othello'?
e: Iago, Othello's ancient (ensign), plots Othello's downfall out of professional resentment over Cassio's promotion and sheer malice, which S.T. Coleridge famously termed "motiveless malignity."

q: Who is the rightful Duke of Milan and magician-protagonist of Shakespeare's last solo play 'The Tempest'?
e: Prospero, usurped by his brother Antonio, lives on a remote island with his daughter Miranda and commands the airy spirit Ariel and the savage Caliban. His final renunciation of magic is often read as Shakespeare's farewell to the stage.

q: In 'The Merchant of Venice', who disguises herself as the young doctor of law 'Balthazar' to save Antonio from Shylock's bond?
e: Portia of Belmont disguises herself as Balthazar in the Trial Scene (Act IV, Scene 1) and delivers the celebrated "The quality of mercy is not strained" speech before defeating Shylock on a legal technicality (no drop of Christian blood).

q: Who delivers the famous funeral oration beginning "Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears" in 'Julius Caesar'?
e: Mark Antony delivers this masterwork of ironic rhetoric in Act III, Scene 2, repeatedly calling Brutus "an honourable man" until he turns the Roman plebeians against the conspirators.

q: Which of King Lear's three daughters refuses to flatter him in the love-test (Act I, Scene 1) and replies simply, "Nothing, my lord"?
e: Cordelia, Lear's youngest and most devoted daughter, refuses hollow flattery ("I love your majesty according to my bond; no more nor less"), prompting Lear to disinherit her and divide Britain between Goneril and Regan.

q: Who praised Shakespeare in the First Folio (1623) prefatory poem with the words, "He was not of an age, but for all time"?
e: Ben Jonson wrote the famous eulogy "To the Memory of My Beloved, the Author Mr. William Shakespeare" in the 1623 First Folio, also calling him "Sweet Swan of Avon" and noting his "small Latin and less Greek."

q: In 'As You Like It', which character delivers the famous "All the world's a stage" (Seven Ages of Man) speech?
e: The melancholic lord Jaques delivers the "Seven Ages of Man" speech in Act II, Scene 7, in the Forest of Arden. The play's primary source is Thomas Lodge's pastoral romance 'Rosalynde' (1590).

q: Who finally kills Macbeth in single combat at the end of 'Macbeth', fulfilling the Witches' prophecy?
e: Macduff, Thane of Fife, reveals he "was from his mother's womb untimely ripp'd" (delivered by Caesarean section), fulfilling the Second Apparition's prophecy that "none of woman born shall harm Macbeth."

q: Which contemporary playwright attacked Shakespeare in 'Greene's Groats-Worth of Wit' (1592) as an "upstart crow, beautified with our feathers"?
e: University Wit Robert Greene made this jealous attack in 1592, parodying a line from 'Henry VI, Part 3' ("O tiger's heart wrapp'd in a woman's hide") as "Tyger's hart wrapt in a Players hyde."

q: In 'Macbeth', which short scene immediately follows King Duncan's murder and was famously praised by Thomas De Quincey for providing comic relief and heightening tragic tension?
e: The Porter Scene (Act II, Scene 3) features the drunken Porter imagining himself as keeper of Hell-Gate. De Quincey's 1823 essay 'On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth' analyzes how the knocking restores the ordinary world after the horror of regicide.

q: In 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', which mischievous fairy transforms Nick Bottom's head into that of an ass?
e: Puck (Robin Goodfellow), servant to Fairy King Oberon, gives the weaver Bottom an ass's head in Act III, Scene 1, so that Queen Titania (under the love-in-idleness flower's spell) falls in love with him.

q: Which critic coined the term 'Problem Plays' (1896) for Shakespeare's 'All's Well That Ends Well', 'Measure for Measure', and 'Troilus and Cressida'?
e: Frederick S. Boas introduced the term 'Problem Plays' in 'Shakspere and His Predecessors' (1896), borrowing the phrase from Henrik Ibsen's social dramas to describe these morally ambiguous dark comedies.

q: "Ripeness is all" — this famous stoic line is spoken by Edgar in which Shakespearean tragedy?
e: Edgar comforts his blind father Gloucester in Act V, Scene 2 of 'King Lear' with "Men must endure / Their going hence, even as their coming hither: / Ripeness is all." Compare Hamlet's "The readiness is all" (Act V, Scene 2).

q: Which Shakespearean sonnet opens with the immortal question, "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?"
e: Sonnet 18 celebrates the eternalizing power of verse ("So long lives this, and this gives life to thee"). Sonnet 116 begins "Let me not to the marriage of true minds"; Sonnet 130 begins "My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun."

q: What was Shakespeare's primary historical source for all three Roman Plays ('Julius Caesar', 'Antony and Cleopatra', and 'Coriolanus')?
o: Sir Thomas North's translation of Plutarch's Lives
e: Shakespeare relied closely on Sir Thomas North's 1579 English translation (via Jacques Amyot's French) of Plutarch's 'Parallel Lives'. For British histories and Macbeth/King Lear, he used Raphael Holinshed's 'Chronicles' (1577/1587).

q: In 'Hamlet', what is the name of the play-within-the-play that Hamlet stages to "catch the conscience of the King"?
e: In Act III, Scene 2, Hamlet inserts lines into 'The Murder of Gonzago', nicknaming it 'The Mousetrap'. When the player pours poison into the sleeping king's ear, Claudius rises in guilt, confirming the Ghost's accusation.

q: In 'The Winter's Tale', which famous stage direction occurs in Act III, Scene 3, sealing the fate of Antigonus?
e: After abandoning the infant Perdita on the seacoast of Bohemia on King Leontes's orders, Antigonus meets his end with Shakespeare's most celebrated stage direction: "Exit, pursued by a bear." The play's source is Robert Greene's 'Pandosto' (1588).

q: In 'King Lear', who disguises himself as the mad beggar 'Poor Tom' (Tom o' Bedlam) to escape his father Gloucester's wrath?
e: Edgar, legitimate son of Gloucester, is framed by his illegitimate half-brother Edmund and flees disguised as 'Poor Tom'. Similarly, the loyal Earl of Kent disguises himself as 'Caius' to keep serving Lear.

q: Who called Shakespeare "the largest and most comprehensive soul" among all modern and perhaps ancient poets in 'An Essay of Dramatic Poesy' (1668)?
e: John Dryden praised Shakespeare in 'An Essay of Dramatic Poesy' (1668), contrasting him with Ben Jonson ("I admire him, but I love Shakespeare").

q: In 'As You Like It', what male disguise name does Rosalind adopt in the Forest of Arden?
e: Rosalind disguises herself as the shepherd 'Ganymede' while her cousin Celia adopts the name 'Aliena'. Viola disguises as 'Cesario' in 'Twelfth Night', and Portia as 'Balthazar' in 'The Merchant of Venice'.

q: "Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale / Her infinite variety" — Enobarbus speaks these celebrated lines about whom?
e: Domitius Enobarbus speaks this famous tribute to Cleopatra in Act II, Scene 2 of 'Antony and Cleopatra' (c. 1606–07), right after his dazzling description of her golden barge on the River Cydnus.

q: In 'Macbeth', who speaks the nihilistic "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow" soliloquy upon hearing of Lady Macbeth's death?
e: In Act V, Scene 5, Macbeth responds to Seyton's news ("The Queen, my lord, is dead") with "Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player / That struts and frets his hour upon the stage... a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing."

q: In which year did the Globe Theatre (built on the South Bank of the Thames in 1599) burn down during a performance of 'Henry VIII'?
e: On 29 June 1613, a theatrical cannon misfired during a performance of 'Henry VIII' ('All Is True'), igniting the thatched roof and burning the Globe Theatre to the ground; it was rebuilt in 1614.

q: Which comic character in 'Twelfth Night' is tricked by a forged letter from Maria into wearing yellow stockings and cross-garters?
e: Malvolio, Olivia's puritanical steward, falls for Maria's forged letter (pretending Olivia loves him), prompting Sir Toby's famous rebuke: "Dost thou think, because thou art virtuous, there shall be no more cakes and ale?"

q: Who remarked in 'Preface to Shakespeare' (1765) that "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men"?
e: Dr. Samuel Johnson's 'Preface to Shakespeare' (1765) defended Shakespeare's mingling of tragedy and comedy and his violation of the Neoclassical Unities of Time and Place while noting his weakness for "quibbles" (puns).

q: Which early Shakespearean tragedy is considered a Senecan revenge tragedy noted for its extreme violence and gruesome banquet?
e: 'Titus Andronicus' (c. 1592–94), possibly co-written with George Peele, is Shakespeare's earliest and bloodiest revenge tragedy, modeled on Seneca's 'Thyestes' and Ovid's tale of Philomela.

q: In 'Hamlet', who is Polonius's son who returns from France to avenge his father's death and duels Hamlet with a poisoned rapier?
e: Laertes serves as a foil to Hamlet — quick to act in vengeance without hesitation — while Prince Fortinbras of Norway acts as another decisive foil and claims the Danish throne at the end.

q: "Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once." Who speaks these lines in 'Julius Caesar'?
e: Julius Caesar speaks these lines to his wife Calpurnia in Act II, Scene 2, dismissing her ominous nightmares and the augurers' warnings before going to the Senate House on the Ides of March (15 March).

q: In his 1919 essay 'Hamlet and His Problems', which critic called 'Hamlet' "most certainly an artistic failure" for lacking an adequate 'objective correlative'?
e: T.S. Eliot coined the famous critical term 'objective correlative' in 'Hamlet and His Problems' (1919), arguing that Hamlet's disgust is in excess of the facts (his mother Gertrude is not an adequate objective correlative for his emotion).

q: Edward Dowden divided Shakespeare's dramatic career into four famous periods. What name did Dowden give to the FOURTH period (1608–1613, the Romances)?
e: Edward Dowden ('Shakspere: A Critical Study of His Mind and Art', 1875) named the four periods: (1) In the Workshop (early plays), (2) In the World (histories & mature comedies), (3) Out of the Depths (great tragedies & problem plays), and (4) On the Heights (late romances: Pericles, Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale, The Tempest).

q: Which group of sonnets (Sonnets 78–86) in Shakespeare's 1609 sequence refers to a competing poet vying for the Fair Youth's patronage (often speculated to be George Chapman or Christopher Marlowe)?
e: Sonnets 1–17 are the 'Procreation Sonnets' urging the Fair Youth to marry; Sonnets 78–86 form the 'Rival Poet' sequence; Sonnets 127–152 address the 'Dark Lady'.

q: In 'Measure for Measure', who is the hypocritically puritanical deputy left in charge of Vienna by Duke Vincentio, who tries to blackmail Isabella?
e: Angelo enforces Vienna's dormant fornication laws against Claudio while secretly demanding the novice Isabella's chastity in exchange for her brother's life, foiled by the disguised Duke's 'bed-trick' involving Mariana.

q: Which of the following Shakespearean plays is NOT correctly matched with its primary literary source?
o: Hamlet — Saxo Grammaticus / François de Belleforest
The Tempest — Sir Thomas North's Plutarch
e: 'The Tempest' has NO single narrative source (it draws loosely on William Strachey's 1610 Bermuda shipwreck letter and Montaigne's essay 'Of the Cannibals', translated by John Florio), NOT Plutarch.

q: Which TWO plays by William Shakespeare are famously noted by critics for strictly observing all three Classical Unities (Time, Place, and Action)?
o: The Comedy of Errors and The Tempest
Othello and As You Like It
e: 'The Comedy of Errors' (Shakespeare's shortest play, ~1,787 lines, modeled on Plautus's 'Menaechmi') and 'The Tempest' (unfolding in ~3–4 hours on a single island) uniquely observe the classical unities of time, place, and action.

q: Who famously wrote "I cannot read King Lear on the stage... the Lear of Shakespeare cannot be acted" in his 1811 essay 'On the Tragedies of Shakespeare'?
e: Charles Lamb argued in 1811 that the sublime mental agony of 'King Lear' loses its vastness in physical stage representation; he also co-authored 'Tales from Shakespeare' (1807) with his sister Mary Lamb.

q: Which is Shakespeare's LONGEST play by line count (~4,042 lines) and which is his SHORTEST tragedy (~2,107 lines)?
o: Antony and Cleopatra (longest) and Julius Caesar (shortest)
e: 'Hamlet' is Shakespeare's longest play overall (~4,042 lines, with Hamlet having the largest speaking role), while 'Macbeth' is his shortest tragedy (~2,107 lines) and 'The Comedy of Errors' is his shortest play overall.

q: John Keats coined the celebrated critical concept of 'Negative Capability' in a December 1817 letter to his brothers, citing which writer as its supreme exemplar?
e: Keats defined Negative Capability as being "capable of being in uncertainties, Mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact & reason," naming Shakespeare as the "man of achievement" who possessed it enormously (in contrast to Coleridge).

q: In 'The Merchant of Venice', what are the three caskets from which Portia's suitors must choose, and which casket contains Portia's portrait?
o: Gold, Silver, and Lead — Lead casket
Gold, Silver, and Iron — Silver casket
Gold, Bronze, and Lead — Gold casket
Diamond, Silver, and Lead — Lead casket
e: The Prince of Morocco chooses Gold ("Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire"), the Prince of Arragon chooses Silver ("as much as he deserves"), and Bassanio correctly chooses Lead ("must give and hazard all he hath").

q: "As flies to wanton boys are we to th' gods; / They kill us for their sport." Which blinded character utters these bleak lines in 'King Lear'?
e: The Earl of Gloucester speaks these despairing lines in Act IV, Scene 1, after Cornwall and Regan gouge out his eyes ("Out, vile jelly!"), highlighting the play's dark vision of cosmic cruelty.

q: Which late play (1613), based on Chaucer's 'The Knight's Tale', is widely recognized as a collaboration between William Shakespeare and John Fletcher?
e: 'The Two Noble Kinsmen' (printed 1634, credited on its title page to Fletcher and Shakespeare) and 'Henry VIII' (1613) — plus the lost play 'Cardenio' — were late collaborations with John Fletcher, who succeeded Shakespeare as chief playwright of the King's Men.

q: In 'Coriolanus', who is the formidable Roman mother of Caius Marcius Coriolanus who persuades him not to burn Rome?
e: Volumnia kneels before her exiled son Coriolanus in Act V, Scene 3, winning peace for Rome at the cost of his life ("O my mother, mother! O! / You have won a happy victory to Rome; / But, for your son, believe it, O, believe it, / Most dangerously you have with him prevail'd").

q: Who coined the famous phrase "Shakespeare's tragic flaw" (hamartia) and emphasized that "Character is destiny" in 'Shakespearean Tragedy' (1904)?
e: Andrew Cecil Bradley's 'Shakespearean Tragedy' (1904) analyzed Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, and Macbeth through character psychology and tragic flaw, though later New Critics like L.C. Knights ('How Many Children Had Lady Macbeth?', 1933) challenged his character-centric method.

q: "We are such stuff / As dreams are made on, and our little life / Is rounded with a sleep." In which act and play does Prospero utter these lines?
o: Act V, Scene 1 of The Winter's Tale
Act IV, Scene 1 of The Tempest
Act III, Scene 2 of A Midsummer Night's Dream
e: Prospero speaks these transcendent lines in Act IV, Scene 1 of 'The Tempest' right after abruptly ending the betrothal masque of Iris, Ceres, and Juno upon remembering Caliban's conspiracy.
